title: The pope who put a dead pope on trial
hook: A pope put a dead pope on trial.
summary: In 897 Pope Stephen VI had his dead predecessor Formosus dug up and tried in court; it ended with Stephen jailed and a ban on trials of the dead.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pope Formosus and Pope Stephen VI (VII): Formosus died 896; posthumous trial in 897 (the Cadaver Synod); Stephen imprisoned and died in 897.
Catholic Encyclopedia, Pope Formosus: body exhumed, tried, declared guilty; later popes Theodore II and John IX annulled the verdict in 898.

lines.text: A pope put a dead pope on trial.
In eight ninety-seven, Stephen the Sixth had Formosus dug up.
The body was dressed in robes and seated on a throne.
A young deacon had to answer the questions for him.
The dead pope was found guilty.
But Romans were outraged, and Stephen was jailed, where he died.
lines.caps: But Romans were *outraged, | Stephen was *jailed, | where he *died

lines.text: Within two years, a new pope banned trials of the dead.
lines.caps: Within *two years, | a new pope *banned | trials of the *dead

lines.text: Yes, someone had to write that law.

post.caption:
In 897 a dead pope was dug up, seated on a throne and put on trial. It is called the Cadaver Synod.
Which weird law do you think should never have needed writing?
